Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

The folder stayed open on the counter, and anyone could read the names and copy down the door code. In February, the studio committee agreed to move the list into a locked cabinet and keep one current copy with the duty coordinator. The change was about limiting access to the information, not changing who was entitled to use the studio.

Mara, who manages the room calendar, collected the names from the three groups and checked them against the membership records. She sent each person a short message asking them to confirm the spelling of their name, their usual visiting hours, and whether they needed access to the side entrance. Two people replied that they no longer used the studio, so Mara left them off the proposed list. A third person asked to be removed from the email chain but did not ask to lose door access; Mara kept that person on the access list and changed the mailing record separately. She wrote in her notebook, “Being left off the messages is not the same as being removed from the building list.”

The first draft had a few practical problems. It included a visiting tutor whose contract had ended, and it left out Inez, who had renewed her membership the previous week. The pottery group also had a shared equipment key, which did not give every member permission to enter the studio outside booked hours. Mara checked those details with the group leads instead of treating the key record as proof of general access. She also asked the evening-class coordinator to confirm the dates of the next course, since two temporary assistants would need entry only while that course was running. One assistant had not yet confirmed which evenings she could attend, so Mara marked her access as pending rather than guessing.

At the committee meeting, people agreed on a simple rule for the list: include current members and named workers who need the room for an assigned task, but do not add visitors just because they have been inside before. A member may ask for another person to be removed, but the request must identify that person and give a reason for the committee to review. The group did not make any automatic removals based on a complaint alone. If the concern involved immediate safety, the duty coordinator could temporarily pause a code or arrange for someone to meet the person at the entrance while the committee considered what to do. No one at the meeting said that a temporary pause would settle the underlying question.

1. The working copy has four columns: name, access category, start date, and review date. The category says “member,” “assigned worker,” or “temporary course access.” For course access, the review date is the final scheduled class, unless the coordinator confirms an extension. Mara keeps the reason for a special arrangement in a separate restricted note, rather than writing personal details beside everyone’s name. The committee can review that note when needed, but it is not displayed with the day-to-day access sheet. A blank review date means that someone still needs to confirm it; it does not mean that access lasts forever.

The removal request from the print room arrived on a Thursday afternoon. It named Colin, a former volunteer, and said he had been receiving calendar notices after his volunteering ended. The request asked for him to be taken off the notices and the access list. Mara confirmed that his volunteer assignment had finished in January, removed his email address from the calendar group, and sent the access question to the committee because Colin still had a current studio membership. The chair replied that membership status needed to be checked before any access decision was recorded. Until that check was complete, Mara changed no membership category and did not tell the print room that Colin had been removed from the building list.

Colin answered Mara’s note the next morning. He said he had not used the studio since January and was willing to return the old equipment key, but he wanted to keep his membership while he decided whether to join a spring project. Mara recorded his statement and arranged a key return with the front desk. She did not interpret his willingness to return the equipment key as a request to cancel his membership. The committee secretary checked the payment record and found that his membership was current through June. At the next meeting, the committee discussed the request, reviewed the membership rule, and asked Mara to contact Colin again before making a change to his door access. The list therefore continued to show his existing member status during that review.

A separate issue came up when the evening class changed rooms for one week because of a ventilation repair. The two assistants needed access to the side entrance on the original dates, but the class itself would meet in the downstairs room. The facilities manager confirmed that the studio door code would still be required to collect teaching materials, while the downstairs entrance used a different key. Mara kept the assistants’ temporary entries on the list through the last scheduled class and added a note that the room location had changed for that week. She did not extend their access beyond the course dates simply because the repair might run late; any extension would need a new date confirmed by the coordinator.

By the end of the month, the blue folder was empty and the locked cabinet held the current working copy. The duty coordinator checked the sheet at opening and closing, and Mara stored the previous version in a sealed envelope marked with its date so that changes could be traced if someone asked. The committee had not decided whether to replace the door code, so the existing code remained in use. At the next membership review, the secretary planned to compare the list with renewals and course schedules, including Colin’s status if he had not contacted Mara before then.
